question: Child protection is an essential obligation of Member States and a fundamental principle guiding EU action, as stated in Article 3(3) of the Treaty on European Union and Article 24 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights.

It is estimated that more than 750 000 children in the EU live under some form of protection measure1, a growing figure that highlights the need for robust, rights-based systems that prioritise family-based care and guarantee the best interests of the child. To understand the scope of this reality and design effective policies, it is essential to have common data and indicators.

The Fundamental Rights Agency (FRA)2 notes that protection systems are complex and that no common understanding currently exists among states. Meanwhile, the Commission, through Recommendation (EU) 2024/1238, formulated key guidelines to promote integrated child protection systems and advance deinstitutionalisation. Therefore: 1.
How does the Commission intend to monitor these recommendations?
Does it plan to submit any proposal to improve data availability?

UNICEF, Children in alternative care: Comparable statistics to monitor progress on deinstitutionalisation across the European Union, 2021: https://www.unicef.org/eca/media/19756/file/UNICEFDataCare%20Policy%20Brief.pdf. 2 FRA, Mapping Child Protection Systems in the EU – Update 2023: https://fra.europa.eu/en/publication/2024/mapping-child-protection-systems-eu-update-2023. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.11.2026) While child protection is anchored in the EU acquis, child protection systems remain primarily a Member State competence. The Commission Recommendation (EU) 2024/12381 provides a framework guiding Member States when developing integrated, child-rights-based child protection systems.
Deinstitutionalisation and the transition towards quality family and community-based care and services, with due regard to the best interests of the child are a key emphasis of the Recommendation.

As regards monitoring the implementation of the Recommendation, the Commission follows developments in Member States through dialogue, mutual learning and the exchange of good practices, notably through the EU Network for Children’s Rights2. The Commission will launch on 19 November 2026, the Mutual Learning Programme 2026–2028 to promote evidence-informed policymaking in support of the Recommendation.

Relevant EU funding instruments, including the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values Programme-Daphne strand3 and the Technical Support Instrument4, further support Member States in implementing reforms towards integrated child protection systems.

As regards data, the Commission is implementing a data methodology project on violence against children, which complements the ongoing work of Eurostat, the Fundamental Rights Agency and national authorities to enhance the availability, quality and comparability of relevant information on children, in full respect of data‑protection and ethical rules.
